"============================================================
PROJECT NAME: WILD SURVIVAL – THE LOST ISLAND
COMPLETE 3D OPEN WORLD SURVIVAL GAME

PROJECT TYPE:
Professional 3D Open World Survival Adventure.

PLATFORM:
Android Smartphones.

GAME MODE:
Single Player – Fully Offline.

CAMERA:
Third-Person 3D Camera.

GRAPHICS:
High-quality Stylized Realistic 3D.

GAME ENGINE:
Unity 6 with Universal Render Pipeline (URP).

TARGET:
A fully playable, optimized Android survival game with a detailed open world, realistic 3D characters, intelligent wildlife, crafting, construction, combat, exploration and a complete survival system.

============================================================
PART 1: COMPLETE GAME VISION AND DESIGN RULES

1.1 GAME CONCEPT

Create an immersive open-world survival game where the main character gets stranded on a mysterious tropical island after an airplane crash.

The player begins with almost nothing.

They must explore the island, collect materials, discover food and water, craft tools, build a shelter, hunt animals, defend themselves against dangerous creatures and gradually establish a complete survival base.

The island must feel like a real living world.

The player should always have meaningful activities to perform.

1.2 GRAPHICS REQUIREMENTS

The entire playable world must be 3D.

This includes:

- Player character.
- Human characters.
- Animals.
- Zombies.
- Trees.
- Grass.
- Flowers.
- Rocks.
- Mountains.
- Rivers.
- Oceans.
- Buildings.
- Caves.
- Weapons.
- Tools.
- Furniture.
- Vehicles and environmental objects.

Use 3D models with appropriate textures, materials, lighting, shadows, collision and animations.

2D is permitted only for the HUD, menus, inventory icons, maps, buttons and interface elements.

DO NOT:

- Use 2D sprites as the actual world or characters.
- Use flat photographs instead of 3D environments.
- Mix unrelated cartoon, anime and realistic art styles.
- Use low-quality placeholder objects in the finished game.
- Make the entire environment look excessively shiny.
- Use extreme cinematic blur that hides gameplay details.

1.3 VISUAL QUALITY

Use a stylized-realistic visual direction.

The world should have:

- Natural colors.
- Detailed materials.
- Realistic environmental proportions.
- Soft but visible shadows.
- Natural sunlight.
- Detailed vegetation.
- Attractive water.
- Consistent texture quality.
- Smooth character animations.
- Beautiful environmental depth.

The game should look visually rich without requiring excessively powerful hardware.

1.4 CORE GAMEPLAY RULES

Every major gameplay system must interact with other systems.

Examples:

Cutting a tree must produce wood.

Wood must enter the inventory.

Wood must be usable for crafting.

Crafting must consume the required materials.

A crafted axe must be equippable.

The axe must be usable to cut another tree.

A building must consume construction materials.

A constructed shelter must provide protection from rain and some environmental dangers.

Never implement a feature that exists only visually without its corresponding gameplay functionality.

============================================================
PART 2: WORLD MAP AND GEOGRAPHICAL DESIGN

2.1 WORLD SIZE

Create a large explorable island with a recommended initial playable terrain size of approximately 4 km x 4 km.

Do not make the entire world empty.

Divide the island into eight carefully designed geographical regions.

Each region must have a clear identity, visual appearance, resource distribution and purpose.

2.2 ISLAND GEOGRAPHY

The island should have:

- A large coastline.
- Central mountain ranges.
- Dense tropical forests.
- Rivers flowing from elevated areas.
- Several freshwater lakes.
- Underground caves.
- Rocky cliffs.
- Swamp areas.
- Abandoned settlements.
- Hidden valleys.

The central mountain range should be visible from several distant locations to help players understand the geography.

The coastline should surround the island naturally.

Avoid perfectly circular terrain or artificial-looking biome borders.

2.3 REGION ONE: CRASH BEACH

This is the player's starting location.

ENVIRONMENT:

Create a beautiful tropical beach with:

- Soft sandy ground.
- Palm trees.
- Coconut trees.
- Small coastal rocks.
- Driftwood.
- Beach grass.
- Seashells.
- Ocean waves.
- Shallow water.
- Distant ocean horizon.

AIRPLANE WRECKAGE:

Place a crashed passenger airplane near the starting beach.

Include:

- Broken fuselage.
- Detached airplane wings.
- Damaged seats.
- Scattered luggage.
- Broken windows.
- Metal debris.
- Emergency supplies.
- Damaged aircraft parts.

The wreckage must look like the result of an actual crash.

Do not place every object in a perfectly organized manner.

Some objects should be partially buried in sand, while others should be scattered naturally.

STARTING RESOURCES:

Place a small number of:

- Collectible stones.
- Branches.
- Coconuts.
- Palm leaves.
- Driftwood.
- Basic emergency supplies.

Do not provide unlimited resources at the starting point.

The player must explore to obtain more materials.

2.4 REGION TWO: GREEN TROPICAL FOREST

Create a dense tropical forest with several layers of vegetation.

CANOPY:
Tall tropical trees with detailed branches and leaf clusters.

MIDDLE LAYER:
Medium-sized trees, bushes and vines.

GROUND LAYER:
Ferns, grass, flowers, roots, mushrooms and fallen leaves.

GROUND DETAILS:
Small stones, branches, roots, exposed soil and natural vegetation.

Add narrow animal paths and occasional open clearings.

FOREST DESIGN RULES:

- Trees should have different heights and shapes.
- Avoid identical repeated tree arrangements.
- Do not place trees in perfect rows.
- Keep enough space for player movement.
- Create some dense areas that are difficult to navigate.
- Create occasional open areas where players can build.
- Do not block every pathway with vegetation.

RESOURCE DISTRIBUTION:

Wood, branches, leaves, fruits, fiber, mushrooms and medicinal plants.

WILDLIFE:

Deer, rabbits, wolves, wild boars and birds.

2.5 REGION THREE: ROCKY HILLS

Create elevated rocky terrain with natural slopes.

Include:

- Large rock formations.
- Small collectible stones.
- Exposed mineral deposits.
- Rocky pathways.
- Cliff edges.
- Sparse vegetation.
- Small caves.
- Mountain streams.

Create visually clear differences between normal stone, iron ore and other mineral deposits.

The player must be able to identify collectible minerals.

Do not make every rock collectible.

Some rocks should be decorative environmental objects.

2.6 REGION FOUR: DARK CAVE

Create a network of underground cave systems.

CAVE DESIGN:

- Narrow entrance.
- Large underground chambers.
- Uneven stone walls.
- Stalactites.
- Stalagmites.
- Underground pools.
- Small tunnels.
- Dead ends.
- Hidden chambers.

LIGHTING:

Caves should be naturally dark.

Use subtle ambient lighting and player-controlled light sources.

Place glowing minerals only where appropriate.

Do not make the entire cave brightly illuminated.

Do not make it completely black or impossible to navigate.

GAMEPLAY:

The player should need a torch or lantern to explore deeper areas.

Add rare minerals, coal, stone and dangerous underground creatures.

2.7 REGION FIVE: ABANDONED VILLAGE

Create a small abandoned settlement hidden within the forest.

Include:

- Wooden houses.
- Broken doors.
- Damaged roofs.
- Old furniture.
- Empty containers.
- Broken fences.
- Overgrown pathways.
- Abandoned wells.
- Small storage buildings.

Some buildings should be partially damaged.

Others should remain structurally intact.

Place useful resources inside selected buildings.

Do not fill every house with loot.

Some buildings should be empty to create believable exploration.

2.8 REGION SIX: MOUNTAIN REGION

Create a cold mountainous environment.

Include:

- Pine forests.
- Snow-covered slopes.
- Rocky cliffs.
- Frozen ponds.
- Snow-covered ground.
- Icy streams.
- Mountain caves.

Add temperature challenges.

The player should require appropriate clothing to survive extended exposure to freezing conditions.

Do not place tropical vegetation randomly inside the snowy biome.

2.9 REGION SEVEN: SWAMP

Create a dangerous wetland environment.

Include:

- Shallow muddy water.
- Dark soil.
- Dead trees.
- Mangrove-like vegetation.
- Thick bushes.
- Reeds.
- Water plants.
- Fog.
- Insects.
- Small islands of dry ground.

Make movement slightly slower in deep mud.

Add poisonous plants and rare medicinal resources.

Avoid making the entire swamp uniformly deep water.

Create walkable routes and identifiable safe areas.

2.10 REGION EIGHT: HIDDEN VALLEY

Create a secret geographical region surrounded by cliffs and dense vegetation.

Include:

- Ancient ruins.
- Waterfalls.
- Rare plants.
- Hidden caves.
- Rare minerals.
- Abandoned structures.
- Special wildlife.
- Story-related discoveries.

This region should reward players who explore carefully.

============================================================
PART 3: ENVIRONMENT DESIGN AND OBJECT PLACEMENT RULES

3.1 TERRAIN

Use a detailed 3D terrain system.

Terrain must include:

- Grass.
- Sand.
- Soil.
- Mud.
- Stone.
- Snow.
- Rocky surfaces.

Create smooth transitions between terrain materials.

Do not create sudden unnatural color changes.

Do not use one texture across the entire island.

3.2 TERRAIN ELEVATION

Create natural hills, slopes, cliffs and valleys.

Avoid:

- Completely flat mountains.
- Impossible vertical walking surfaces.
- Sudden terrain holes.
- Floating rocks.
- Unnatural terrain intersections.
- Roads that disappear into mountains.

All important walking routes must have valid collision.

3.3 TREE PLACEMENT

Place trees according to biome type and terrain.

Use a combination of:

- Tall trees.
- Medium trees.
- Small trees.
- Dead trees.
- Fallen trees.

Vary tree height, rotation and appearance.

Do not repeat identical trees next to each other.

Do not place large trees directly in front of important mission objectives.

Do not block the player's camera unnecessarily.

3.4 GRASS AND PLANT PLACEMENT

Grass should grow mainly on suitable soil.

Flowers should appear in small natural groups.

Mushrooms should appear near appropriate damp areas, fallen logs and forest ground.

Ferns should be more common in shaded and humid locations.

Avoid placing hundreds of identical plants in one small area.

3.5 ROCK PLACEMENT

Place large rocks naturally around:

- Hills.
- Cliffs.
- Mountain paths.
- Cave entrances.
- Riverbanks.

Small collectible stones should be clearly distinguishable from large decorative rocks.

Do not allow rocks to float above the ground.

3.6 WATER DESIGN

Create realistic-looking 3D water for:

- Ocean.
- Rivers.
- Lakes.
- Waterfalls.
- Underground pools.

Implement:

- Water surface animation.
- Ripples.
- Shoreline transitions.
- Reflections where performance allows.
- Underwater visibility.
- Swimming interaction.

Do not allow water surfaces to intersect visibly with land.

Water must have proper collision and depth detection.

3.7 OBJECT INTERACTION

Important environmental objects must have interaction rules.

Examples:

A tree:
Can be chopped with a suitable tool.

A coconut:
Can be collected or harvested.

A stone:
Can be picked up.

A mineral deposit:
Can be mined.

A storage box:
Can be opened.

A door:
Can be opened and closed.

A campfire:
Can be ignited and extinguished.

A bed:
Can be used for sleeping.

A workbench:
Can open the crafting interface.

Every interaction must provide clear feedback.

============================================================
PART 4: MAIN CHARACTER MODEL AND CLOTHING

4.1 CHARACTER IDENTITY

Name: Alex Carter.
Age: 26.
Height: 5 feet 11 inches.
Body: Athletic.
Skin: Medium tan.
Hair: Short messy dark brown.
Eyes: Dark brown.
Face: Natural jawline and expressive facial features.
Special detail: Small scar near left eyebrow.

4.2 STARTING CLOTHING

Olive-green half-sleeve survival shirt.

Dark grey fitted undershirt.

Dark brown cargo trousers with multiple pockets.

Brown hiking boots with thick soles.

Fingerless leather gloves.

Brown utility belt.

Medium olive backpack with adjustable straps.

Black digital watch.

Clothing must have:

- Realistic folds.
- Visible stitching.
- Proper material roughness.
- Natural fabric thickness.
- Correct body fitting.
- No visible clipping.

4.3 CLOTHING CONDITION

Clothing should react to gameplay.

Examples:

After rain:
Clothes should appear wet.

After walking through mud:
Lower trousers and boots may become dirty.

After combat:
Small scratches and dirt may appear.

After extended use:
Equipment may visually show wear.

These effects should be subtle and should not damage visual readability.

4.4 CHARACTER CUSTOMIZATION

Allow changing:

- Hairstyles.
- Shirts.
- Pants.
- Shoes.
- Gloves.
- Backpacks.
- Helmets.
- Armor.
- Accessories.

All clothing must correctly fit the character's skeleton and body proportions.

Do not allow incompatible equipment to overlap visibly.

4.5 CHARACTER BODY SYSTEM

Implement:

- Character skeleton.
- Full-body rigging.
- Finger articulation.
- Facial animation.
- Head rotation.
- Shoulder movement.
- Elbow and knee deformation.
- Foot placement.

Use consistent proportions in every animation.

============================================================
PART 5: PLAYER MOVEMENT AND PHYSICS

5.1 MOVEMENT CONTROLLER

Implement a responsive third-person character controller.

The player must be able to:

- Walk.
- Run.
- Sprint.
- Jump.
- Crouch.
- Sneak.
- Swim.
- Climb selected objects.

5.2 MOVEMENT SPEED

Suggested starting values:

Walking: 2.2 metres per second.

Running: 4 metres per second.

Sprinting: 6 metres per second.

Crouching: 1.5 metres per second.

Swimming: 1.8 metres per second.

These values should be configurable.

5.3 MOVEMENT RULES

Character movement must respect:

- Terrain slopes.
- Ground collision.
- Obstacles.
- Stamina.
- Movement state.
- Water depth.
- Animations.

DO NOT:

- Allow the player to walk through walls.
- Allow walking through large trees.
- Allow movement through closed doors.
- Allow unlimited sprinting without stamina.
- Allow jumping infinitely.
- Allow walking normally underwater.
- Allow the character to become stuck on tiny terrain details.
- Allow the player to move while a blocking interface prevents gameplay.

5.4 JUMP SYSTEM

Jumping must include:

- Ground detection.
- Jump input.
- Takeoff animation.
- Air movement.
- Landing animation.
- Landing sound.

Prevent repeated jumps while airborne.

Allow jumping only when the player is in an appropriate movement state.

5.5 SWIMMING

When the player enters sufficiently deep water:

Switch to swimming movement.

Implement:

- Surface swimming.
- Underwater movement.
- Swimming stamina.
- Breath or oxygen meter.
- Water entry animation.
- Water exit animation.

Do not allow walking animations to continue while swimming.

============================================================
PART 6: THIRD-PERSON CAMERA SYSTEM

Create a smooth camera positioned behind and slightly above the player.

DEFAULT CAMERA:
Approximately 4 metres behind the character.

FEATURES:

- Touchscreen camera rotation.
- Adjustable sensitivity.
- Zoom in.
- Zoom out.
- Collision detection.
- Smooth follow.
- Terrain-aware positioning.
- Camera recentering.
- Combat camera behavior.

CAMERA RULES:

Do not allow the camera to pass through walls or large objects.

Do not allow the camera to remain inside the character model.

Do not create sudden camera jumps.

Do not make camera rotation interfere with the movement joystick.

Allow the player to see nearby enemies and environmental threats.

============================================================
PART 7: INTERACTION SYSTEM

Create one universal interaction system.

When the player approaches an interactable object, show a contextual interaction prompt.

Examples:

Tree:
\"Chop Tree\"

Stone:
\"Collect Stone\"

Workbench:
\"Open Crafting\"

Storage:
\"Open Storage\"

Door:
\"Open Door\"

Campfire:
\"Light Fire\"

Bed:
\"Sleep\"

The interaction system must check:

- Player distance.
- Object availability.
- Required tool.
- Required materials.
- Current player state.
- Object state.

Only show actions that can actually be performed.

Do not show \"Chop Tree\" when the player has no usable tool if the design requires a tool.

Do not allow interacting with objects through solid walls.

Do not trigger multiple interactions from one tap.

Add clear success and failure feedback.

============================================================
PART 8: RESOURCE GATHERING

Implement gathering for:

WOOD:
Obtained by chopping trees and collecting branches.

STONE:
Obtained from collectible stones and mining deposits.

FIBER:
Obtained from specific plants.

LEAVES:
Obtained from selected vegetation.

FRUITS:
Obtained from fruit-bearing plants.

MUSHROOMS:
Collected from suitable forest locations.

IRON:
Obtained by mining iron ore.

COAL:
Obtained from underground mineral deposits.

RESOURCE GATHERING RULES:

- Every resource must have a defined source.
- Every resource must have a collection animation.
- Collection must consume time.
- Tool quality should affect gathering speed.
- Some resources must require specific tools.
- Inventory capacity must be respected.

After gathering, update the resource inventory immediately.

Do not give unlimited materials from a single object.

Do not allow resources to appear inside the player's body.

Do not duplicate items when the player repeatedly taps the interaction button.

============================================================
PART 9: TREE CHOPPING SYSTEM

Create a fully interactive tree chopping system.

Each collectible tree must have:

- Health.
- Tree type.
- Wood yield.
- Required tool.
- Chopping animation.
- Hit detection.
- Damage feedback.

CHOPPING PROCESS:

1. Player equips an axe.
2. Player approaches a suitable tree.
3. Interaction prompt appears.
4. Player starts chopping.
5. Axe animation plays.
6. Hit detection checks the tree.
7. Tree health decreases.
8. Wood resources are generated.
9. At zero health, tree falls.
10. Wood logs become collectible.

TREE FALLING:

Use a controlled falling animation or physics-based fall.

Ensure the tree does not:

- Fall through the terrain.
- Damage unrelated objects.
- Launch the player into the air.
- Block the entire world unexpectedly.

After the tree is cut, use an appropriate stump or fallen-trunk state.

Do not instantly remove every tree without a visible falling process.

============================================================
PART 10: INVENTORY AND ITEM MANAGEMENT

Create a complete inventory with:

- Item grid.
- Item categories.
- Item icons.
- Item names.
- Quantity.
- Weight.
- Durability.
- Description.
- Equipment slots.
- Backpack capacity.
- Quick-access slots.

ITEM CATEGORIES:

Weapons.
Tools.
Materials.
Food.
Clothing.
Armor.
Medical.
Building.
Miscellaneous.

FUNCTIONALITY:

- Select items.
- Move items.
- Split stacks.
- Combine compatible stacks.
- Drop items.
- Equip equipment.
- Unequip equipment.
- Inspect descriptions.
- Use consumable items.
- Transfer items to storage.

INVENTORY RULES:

The player must not carry unlimited weight.

When capacity is reached, display a clear warning.

Do not silently delete items.

Do not duplicate items when moving between inventory and storage.

Do not allow incompatible items to stack.

Do not allow broken equipment to provide full functionality.

============================================================
PART 11: SURVIVAL SYSTEM

Create five primary survival indicators:

HEALTH:
Represents player life.

HUNGER:
Decreases gradually over time and through physical activity.

THIRST:
Decreases gradually and increases with heat and physical activity.

STAMINA:
Used for running, sprinting, jumping, swimming and combat.

TEMPERATURE:
Changes according to biome, weather, clothing and shelter.

ADDITIONAL CONDITIONS:

Bleeding.
Poisoning.
Infection.
Exhaustion.
Cold exposure.
Heat exposure.

SURVIVAL RULES:

- Survival indicators must update consistently.
- Food must restore hunger.
- Water must restore thirst.
- Rest must help recover stamina.
- Appropriate clothing must help regulate temperature.
- Medical supplies must treat appropriate injuries.

Do not instantly kill the player because of a small reduction in hunger or thirst.

Provide warnings before critical conditions.

============================================================
PART 12: FOOD, HUNTING AND COOKING

Create a complete food system.

FOOD SOURCES:

Coconuts.
Berries.
Apples.
Mushrooms.
Vegetables.
Fish.
Raw meat.
Cooked meat.

HUNTING:

Animals must have health, hit detection and appropriate reactions.

Successful hunting must produce appropriate resources.

Do not make every animal aggressive.

Some animals should escape when they detect the player.

COOKING:

Allow players to cook using a campfire or cooking station.

Cooking process:

1. Select suitable food.
2. Approach cooking station.
3. Open cooking interface.
4. Select food.
5. Begin cooking.
6. Show cooking progress.
7. Complete cooking.
8. Place cooked food into inventory.

Do not instantly convert raw food into cooked food without a functional action.

Prevent burning or overcooking if that system is implemented.

============================================================
PART 13: WATER AND DRINKING SYSTEM

Create different water sources:

Ocean water.
River water.
Lake water.
Rainwater.
Stored clean water.

Ocean water should not be drinkable directly.

Potentially contaminated water should require purification.

Implement:

- Water collection.
- Bottle filling.
- Water purification.
- Drinking animation.
- Container capacity.
- Clean water storage.

Do not allow drinking from an empty bottle.

Do not allow unlimited water from a single container.

============================================================
PART 14: CRAFTING SYSTEM

Create a fully functional recipe-based crafting system.

BASIC CRAFTING:

Wooden Spear.
Stone Axe.
Stone Knife.
Wooden Hammer.
Campfire.
Basic Shelter.

ADVANCED CRAFTING:

Iron Axe.
Iron Sword.
Hunting Bow.
Arrows.
Storage Chest.
Workbench.
Fishing Rod.
Leather Armor.

PROFESSIONAL CRAFTING:

Advanced Armor.
Reinforced Weapons.
Advanced Backpack.
Metal Doors.
Defensive Traps.
Advanced Workbench.

Each recipe must define:

- Required materials.
- Required quantity.
- Required crafting station.
- Crafting duration.
- Resulting item.
- Unlock requirement.

CRAFTING RULES:

Only show available crafting options as craftable.

Show missing materials clearly.

Consume materials only when crafting successfully starts or according to a clearly defined transaction system.

Do not consume resources twice.

Do not create free items through repeated button taps.

============================================================
PART 15: BASE BUILDING SYSTEM

Create a complete modular 3D construction system.

BUILDING PARTS:

Wooden Foundation.
Stone Foundation.
Wooden Walls.
Stone Walls.
Windows.
Wooden Doors.
Metal Doors.
Flat Roofs.
Sloped Roofs.
Stairs.
Ladders.
Fences.
Watchtowers.

INTERIOR ITEMS:

Bed.
Storage Chest.
Table.
Chair.
Workbench.
Cooking Station.
Fireplace.
Lantern.
Shelves.

BUILDING PROCESS:

1. Select construction mode.
2. Choose a building part.
3. Display a transparent placement preview.
4. Move the preview.
5. Rotate the preview.
6. Check terrain and collision.
7. Check material availability.
8. Confirm placement.
9. Consume required materials.
10. Construct the object.
11. Save the building.

PLACEMENT RULES:

- Objects must rest on valid surfaces.
- Walls must snap to compatible foundations.
- Roofs must connect to compatible structures.
- Doors must have sufficient opening space.
- Stairs must connect correctly.
- Buildings must not overlap invalid objects.
- Construction must not occur through solid terrain.
- Invalid placements must be clearly indicated.

Do not allow floating buildings.

Do not allow invisible building collisions.

Do not allow free construction without required materials.

============================================================
PART 16: ANIMAL AI

Create independent AI behavior for each animal species.

AI STATES:

Idle.
Wandering.
Eating.
Drinking.
Sleeping.
Detecting.
Escaping.
Chasing.
Attacking.
Returning to territory.

DEER:
Usually avoids the player.

RABBIT:
Escapes quickly and hides.

WOLF:
Can hunt in packs and attack when threatened.

BEAR:
Moves slowly and protects its territory.

WILD BOAR:
Can charge aggressively.

BIRDS:
Fly away when disturbed.

Use navigation that respects terrain and obstacles.

Animals must not:

- Walk through walls.
- Float above terrain.
- Become permanently stuck.
- Teleport unnaturally.
- Attack without a valid target.
- Detect players through unlimited distances.

============================================================
PART 17: ZOMBIE AND ENEMY AI

Create four enemy categories.

NORMAL ZOMBIE:
Slow, basic attacks.

RUNNER ZOMBIE:
Fast movement and chasing.

ARMORED ZOMBIE:
High health and increased protection.

NIGHT CREATURE:
Dangerous enemy found in dark areas.

ENEMY AI STATES:

Idle.
Patrol.
Investigate Sound.
Detect Player.
Chase.
Attack.
Take Damage.
Stagger.
Search.
Return.
Die.

Enemy detection must depend on:

- Distance.
- Visibility.
- Obstacles.
- Sound.
- Player movement.

A player running should make more noise than a player crouching.

Enemies should not see through solid walls.

Enemies should not chase the player across the entire island without a defined reason.

Implement fair combat and readable attack animations.

============================================================
PART 18: COMBAT SYSTEM

Implement real-time third-person combat.

MELEE COMBAT:

Axe attacks.
Spear attacks.
Sword attacks.
Shield blocking.
Dodge movement.

RANGED COMBAT:

Bow aiming.
Arrow release.
Projectile movement.
Collision.
Damage calculation.

COMBAT REQUIREMENTS:

- Proper weapon attachment.
- Attack animations.
- Hit detection.
- Damage calculation.
- Enemy reaction.
- Knockback where appropriate.
- Weapon durability.
- Attack cooldown.
- Player damage feedback.

Do not register damage when a weapon visibly misses.

Do not allow unlimited attack speed.

Do not allow weapons to pass through targets without proper hit detection.

Do not make enemies attack through walls.

============================================================
PART 19: FARMING AND AGRICULTURE

Allow the player to create a small farm near the base.

FARMING PROCESS:

1. Select a farming area.
2. Prepare the soil.
3. Plant a seed.
4. Water the plant.
5. Wait for growth.
6. Harvest the crop.
7. Store or consume the food.

Create multiple crops with different growth requirements.

Plants should grow according to game time.

Do not make crops grow instantly unless a special item or mechanic allows it.

Do not allow farming on unsuitable surfaces.

============================================================
PART 20: DAY AND NIGHT SYSTEM

Create a continuous 24-hour game clock.

6 AM: Sunrise.
8 AM: Morning.
12 PM: Noon.
4 PM: Afternoon.
6 PM: Sunset.
8 PM: Night.
12 AM: Deep Night.
4 AM: Early Morning.

Implement:

- Dynamic sunlight.
- Changing sky colors.
- Moving clouds.
- Moonlight.
- Changing shadows.
- Nighttime visibility.
- Environmental lighting.

Nighttime must feel different from daytime.

The player should need torches, lanterns or campfires in dark areas.

Do not make nighttime completely black.

Do not make daytime excessively bright.

============================================================
PART 21: WEATHER SYSTEM

Implement:

Sunny Weather.
Cloudy Weather.
Light Rain.
Heavy Rain.
Thunderstorm.
Fog.
Wind.
Cold Weather.

Weather must influence:

- Visibility.
- Temperature.
- Environmental sounds.
- Water surfaces.
- Character condition.
- Animal activity.

Rain must have proper particle effects.

Thunderstorms should include occasional lightning.

Do not play thunder sounds continuously.

Do not change from sunny weather to extreme storms every few seconds.

Weather transitions should be gradual and believable.

============================================================
PART 22: AUDIO SYSTEM

Create separate audio categories.

ENVIRONMENT:
Birds, wind, insects, ocean, rivers, rain and thunder.

CHARACTER:
Footsteps, breathing, jumping, landing, swimming and pain reactions.

COMBAT:
Weapon swings, impacts, enemy sounds and attacks.

INTERFACE:
Button sounds, inventory sounds, crafting sounds and notifications.

Use positional 3D audio for animals, enemies, water and environmental events.

Sounds should become quieter with distance.

Do not play every sound at maximum volume.

Avoid repetitive audio loops becoming annoying.

============================================================
PART 23: MOBILE UI AND CONTROLS

Create a professional Android landscape interface.

LEFT SIDE:
Movement joystick.

RIGHT SIDE:

- Character location.

- Inventory.

- Hunger.
- Thirst.

## Objective
- Build a complete, playable mobile-friendly 3D open-world survival game inspired by the supplied “Wild Survival – The Lost Island” specification.

## Requirements
- A real-time 3D experience with a stylized-realistic island, third-person character, survival systems, gathering, crafting, inventory, combat, missions, saving, and Android-oriented controls.
- Prefer functionality and stability over incomplete visual-only features.

## Decisions
- Used a self-contained HTML/CSS/JavaScript web implementation with Three.js rather than Unity.
- Assumed a browser-playable 3D prototype is the appropriate existing-project target.

## Work State
### Completed
- Created the main app shell and professional survival-game HUD in `index.html`.
- Created responsive desktop/mobile styling in `style.css`.
- Began the Three.js game implementation in `game.js`.
- Implemented terrain generation, island shoreline, mountain anchors, trees, palms, rocks, wreckage, resource pickups, lake, animals, player model, and basic systems.
- Implemented starter inventory, recipes, crafting, interaction, UI panels, weather/time labels, and save-related code structure.

### Active
- Completing missing portions of `game.js`, including UI event handlers, movement/camera controls, animation loop, inventory rendering, building placement, save/load, mission progression, and final runtime verification.

### Blocked
- The implementation is not yet completed or verified in a browser; no local build or screenshot verification was performed during this work.

## Next Move
1. Finish `game.js` from the existing state, then test it in a browser.
2. Add and verify movement, camera, keyboard/mobile input, animation, inventory, crafting, and interaction event handlers.
3. Complete save/load and mission objective logic.
4. Run the project and inspect a JPEG screenshot at 1280px or less to reject empty/loading states.
